title: The one who stopped
hook: Angulimala's song: whoever was careless and now is not lights up the world like the moon (Theragatha, Angulimala)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunita the flower-sweeper, bowed to at dawn by gods and called dakkhineyya. Your line was once despised. Today, a man who wasn't looked down on. He was feared.

I have stopped. You stop too. In the old story, those are the Buddha's words to a man running after him with a sword. The man is Angulimala, the bandit named for the garland of fingers he wore. In the sutta he runs as hard as he can and still can't catch up, though the Buddha is only walking. He shouts at him to stop, and gets that answer back. That chase is told in the Middle Length Discourses. Today, the song the Theragatha gives to Angulimala himself, after he stopped.
screen: `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` → `HE RUNS AND CAN'T CATCH UP.` → `TODAY, HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, his name. My name was Harmless, he says, even while I was harming. Now the name is true. I harm no one. The old name had been false. Now it fits. Second, the turn. He looks back on himself as a bandit, swept along like something in a flood, and says he went to the Buddha for refuge. He doesn't dress it up. Third, the line he's remembered for. Whoever was careless before, and afterward is not, lights up the world like the moon set free from a cloud. The same verse stands in the Dhammapada, and Max Müller's old translation gives it like this: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." The clouds were real. The moon doesn't pretend they weren't there. It comes out from behind them. Fourth, the cost. In the sutta, after he becomes a monk, Angulimala goes for alms and people throw clods and stones. He comes back bleeding, his bowl broken, his robe torn. The Buddha tells him to bear it: the fruit of what he did is ripening now, here. So the moon from the cloud isn't a clean slate. It's a turning point, and then a road. Some readers ask whether the story comes too easily, and what of the people he hurt. The text doesn't hide from that. It keeps the light and the stones in the same story.
screen: `HARMLESS: NOW THE NAME IS TRUE.` · `SWEPT ALONG, THEN TAKING REFUGE.` · `THE MOON SET FREE FROM A CLOUD.` · `STONES ON THE ALMS ROUND.` · then, large: `THE MOON FROM THE CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Let one recent, ordinary thing come to mind that you'd like to have done differently, a sharp word, a dropped promise, not the worst thing. Don't pretend it didn't happen, since the clouds were real; just stop, the way Angulimala stopped. Then, on an out-breath, let a small next step come into view, like the moon coming out, without needing to take it yet.
Angulimala. The bandit named for a garland of fingers, who stopped running after the Buddha, became a monk, and sang of the moon set free from a cloud. Today's word.
Your line: the moon from the cloud. Harmless became a true name at last. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In some Theravada countries, monks chant the Angulimala paritta, a protective verse from his story, for women in childbirth, and teachers tell his story when they speak of beginning again.

chat.says: Did Angulimala's past just disappear once he became a monk?
options: No. People threw stones at him, and the Buddha said his deeds were ripening.
Yes. Becoming a monk wiped his past clean, so nothing followed him.
No. The monks made him live outside the order until he'd made amends.
